tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': absolute path (no ~) to the built .app bundle (e.g. /Users/me/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/MyApp-abc123/Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.

schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

.pen files are encrypted: access them only via the MCP tools — never use Read or Grep on .pen files. Follow each tool's input schema exactly.

Make sure you are aware of the .pen schema and the instructions for the execute tool.

While auto mode is active:

You can do much of your work through the Bash tool when it is the simpler route: read files with cat, head, or sed -n, search with grep and find, and make small, mechanical file changes with sed, heredocs, or short scripts instead of the dedicated Read, Edit, or Write tools. The choice is yours: prefer Edit or Write when a shell edit would be fragile, such as exact or multi-line replacements, or sed/awk flags that differ between GNU and BSD/macOS.

1	# ERN — Memory Model Specification v0
2	
3	**Edition: v0 — November 5, 2026. Status: validated and frozen.**
4	
5	**Higher normative authority:** *ERN — Language Charter v0* (October 27, 2026).  
6	This specification defines the normative rules of ERN's memory model. Technical names (`derive`, `transfer`, `issue`, etc.) designate **abstract semantic operations**; they do not constitute syntax decisions.
7	
8	## Validation and Revision Procedure
9	
10	This edition has been validated and acquires normative authority under the ERN Charter v0. Any subsequent semantic change must identify the clauses concerned, justify the change, and preserve the guarantees of the ERN Charter v0. Formal models and proofs are instruments for verifying this specification, not sources of additional rules. Behaviors not determined within its scope are explicitly identified.
11	
12	## Scope
13	
14	This specification defines:
15	
16	- the safe-code contract;
17	- the abstract machine for allocations, bytes, and accesses;
18	- the second-class access discipline;
19	- footprints, authorities, dependencies, frames, and ownership;
20	- read, write, transfer, release, allocation, and pinning transitions;
21	- the normative contract of arenas as a reference library abstraction;
22	- the correspondence obligations between these mechanisms.
23	
24	It does not define syntax, the complete concurrency model, control-flow conventions, the type system, or compiler lowering. The sequential model's scope does not waive the general guarantees of the Charter.
25	
26	---
27	
28	# I. Safe-Behavior Contract
29	
30	The following contract applies to all safe code and all properly encapsulated abstractions, regardless of their concrete memory representation.
31	
32	## 1. Definitions of Safe Behavior
33	
34	**Safe operation:** An operation that imposes no unchecked safety obligation on its user whose violation could compromise the language's guarantees.
35	
36	**Safe code:** Code that executes only safe operations and does not directly assume obligations specific to unsafe operations.
37	
38	**Safe interface:** An interface whose every permitted use preserves the language's guarantees when its implementation is correct.
39	
40	**Safe abstraction:** An abstraction exposing a safe interface; its implementation may use unsafe operations provided it fulfills all their obligations.
41	
42	**Safety obligation:** A condition necessary to preserve the guarantees, explicitly left to the user of an unsafe operation rather than automatically checked by that operation.
43	
44	**Undefined behavior (UB):** Behavior on which the specification imposes no semantic requirements. UB is not a category of recoverable error.
45	
46	## 2. Fundamental Guarantees
47	
48	Every program composed of safe code and correctly implemented safe abstractions must preserve, for **all its permitted executions**, the guarantees of ERN Charter v0 §4.1:
49	
50	1. spatial memory safety;
51	2. temporal memory safety;
52	3. absence of reads of uninitialized values;
53	4. absence of type confusion;
54	5. absence of *data races*.
55	
56	Responsibility for fulfilling internal unsafe obligations belongs to the authors of the abstractions using them, not to their safe callers. These guarantees do not assume a single memory-management runtime.
57	
58	## 3. Behavior Categories
59	
60	- **Defined behavior:** effects and results determined or bounded by the specification, including when it permits multiple results.
61	- **Defined failure:** a situation rejected at runtime with a specified consequence (for example, an error value or controlled termination).
62	- **Implementation-defined behavior:** a choice explicitly permitted by the specification that the implementation must document.
63	- **Undefined behavior (UB):** a situation for which the language imposes no requirements on the behavior of the execution concerned.
64	
65	**Safe code cannot cause any UB, regardless of which language rule is concerned.** A defined failure is not UB. Unspecified situations do not, by default, authorize UB in safe code: they must be explicitly resolved before normative stabilization.
66	
67	## 4. Safety Checks and Optimization
68	
69	Safety conditions may be established statically, checked dynamically **before** the dangerous operation, or guaranteed by the invariants of a correctly implemented safe abstraction.
70	
71	The **dynamic** route is available only when execution actually has the relevant information and an executable procedure capable of deciding the condition **before** the dangerous operation. The logical decidability of a predicate in a proof assistant does not, by itself, constitute an executable check in ERN.
72	
73	Failure of a dynamic check in a safe interface must prevent the dangerous operation and result in a defined failure. An implementation may eliminate a semantically required check only if it demonstrates that the condition holds, without changing the permitted observable behaviors.
74	
75	**Abstract-machine metadata is not mandated at runtime.** Abstract provenance, allocation liveness, per-byte initialization, or a logical authority do not automatically become observable runtime data. A library, instrumented implementation, or specific mechanism may provide the information needed for certain checks; in its absence, guarantees must be established by other means, including static discipline and the contracts of unsafe abstractions.
76	
77	In particular, the absence of a *data race* is a property of concurrent actions and their synchronization relations, not a condition decidable by simply inspecting one access locally. Its precise semantics belongs to the concurrency specification.
78	
79	The existence of an efficient path that avoids an expensive dynamic check is an **evaluation criterion** under Charter §§3.2, 3.3, and 12, not a universal obligation of the memory model.
80	
81	## 5. Contracts of Safe Abstractions
82	
83	A safe interface must never rely on an unchecked discipline imposed on its caller to preserve memory safety. It may impose **functional** preconditions, but their violation by safe code must remain within the language's defined behaviors.
84	
85	Every unsafe operation executed by a safe abstraction must satisfy its contract for all states reachable through permitted use of the interface. A safe interface does not turn an unproved unsafe contract into a guarantee.
86	
87	## 6. Obligations of Unsafe Operations
88	
89	Unsafety qualifies **operations or abstractions**, not a global program mode.
90	
91	An unsafe operation must explicitly state each obligation on which its safety depends. **Violating an obligation explicitly defined as a safety condition constitutes UB.** Other errors are subject to the behavior specified by the operation's contract.
92	
93	Any notation marking an unsafe operation will be determined during syntax design.
94	
95	## 7. Limits of the Guarantees
96	
97	Safe code does not automatically guarantee the absence of memory or resource leaks, deadlocks, or stack overflows. These exclusions do not diminish any guarantee in Section 2. Behavior on resource exhaustion, abnormal termination, or cancellation remains to be specified, without thereby making every safe memory-allocation failure or stack exhaustion defined by default.
98	
99	---
100	
101	# II. Values, Allocations, and Access Representation
102	
103	A value, a place, and a means of access are three distinct notions. The abstract machine distinguishes their existence from their permissions and temporal validity.
104	
105	## 8. Values and Storage Identity
106	
107	A **value** is semantic content; a **place** is a portion of storage capable of containing that content; a **means of access** allows a place to be designated under certain conditions.
108	
109	**Values without intrinsic identity (MVS):** A value has no intrinsic identity. Identity belongs to storage or to a resource designated by the value, not to the value itself. Copying a value, transferring an authority, and accessing a place are semantically distinct operations. The access, consumption, and transfer rules within this model are defined in the following sections; copyability and its typing belong to the appropriate specifications.
110	
111	## 9. Abstract Allocations and Admissible State
112	
113	An abstract allocation has at least:
114	
115	- a **unique identity** within the abstract execution;
116	- an **address space**;
117	- a **base address**;
118	- an **extent** expressed in bytes;
119	- a strictly positive, power-of-two **alignment** satisfied by its base;
120	- a **live** or **dead** state;
121	- abstract offset-indexable storage made up of abstract bytes;
122	- if deallocatable, **deallocation-authority** conditions.
123	
124	An abstract allocation does not necessarily correspond to a library allocator call. The kernel also represents storage with static or automatic duration, whose particular rules will be defined later.
125	
126	**Disjointness of live allocations:** Two distinct live abstract allocations in the **same address space** occupy **disjoint** address ranges. Ranges are half-open: `[base, base + size)`. Two disjoint ranges have an empty intersection. Thus, a zero-sized range overlaps no other range.
127	
128	**Allocation alignment:** Every **registered** abstract allocation, live or dead, has a strictly positive power-of-two alignment; its base is a multiple of that alignment. Valid alignment is a property of admissible states, not merely a creation-time check.
129	
130	Subplaces returned by an arena or a data stack within an allocation are **not automatically new abstract allocations**: they may share its identity and provenance. The abstract machine is *flat*: it introduces no parent–child hierarchy of allocations.
131	
132	The base and extent are modeled over natural numbers in this kernel. Constraints on address width, actually available spaces, and possible overflow of hardware representations are reserved for conversion, layout, and ABI rules; they are not implicitly proved by this mathematical abstraction.
133	
134	**Admissible state and domain:** The abstract state contains registered allocations and a freshness discipline. **Freshness requires that a newly assigned identity has never been assigned before**, even to an allocation that has since died. A monotonically increasing counter is one possible representation, not a language requirement.
135	
136	Admissible states jointly satisfy:
137	
138	- **Well-formedness of identities and freshness:** the preceding discipline is consistent with the registered allocations;
139	- **Disjointness of live allocations:** two distinct live allocations in the same address space do not overlap;
140	- **Alignment:** every registered allocation, live or dead, has valid alignment and an aligned base.
141	
142	Normative memory semantics applies to **admissible states**, namely those satisfying these three properties. An empty state is an admissible initial state and allows reachability proofs; it is **not the only admissible initial state**. An initial configuration supplied by the environment or interoperability may be admissible if it satisfies the required invariants. Establishing such conformity belongs to the applicable initialization or interoperability contract.
143	
144	**Fundamental distinction:** Well-formedness, disjointness, and alignment, as invariants of admissible states, determine the **domain** of the semantics. Their violation in an arbitrary state outside that domain **is not, by itself, a new operational obligation whose violation would be classified as UB**. Relations in a Lean model may nevertheless be mathematically total on such states; their outcomes do not bind the language specification outside the admissible domain.
145	
146	**Raw creation:** In an admissible state, creation of a live allocation requires a fresh identity, valid alignment, a correctly aligned base, and no overlap with any distinct live allocation in the same space. These conditions are **operation** preconditions; their violation by an unsafe raw operation constitutes UB. They are distinct from domain invariants even when one guarantees some of them. Actual resource reservation may additionally fail in a defined manner according to the allocator contract; that case is not equated with a violation of a raw-operation precondition.
147	
148	The abstract machine does not mandate a physical allocation table, `next` counter, or liveness flags at runtime; these are semantic and formalization tools.
149	
150	## 10. Bytes and Initialization
151	
152	This kernel considers **8-bit bytes**, whose initialized value ranges from 0 to 255.
153	
154	An abstract byte is either:
155	
156	- **uninitialized**;
157	- **initialized**, with a byte value and optional provenance information.
158	
159	State is tracked **per byte** to permit partially initialized allocations. In this kernel, the provenance component can be represented by an optional allocation identity; this representation may be enriched by the access discipline. This component is **semantic** information: its existence does not imply a provenance tag physically stored in every byte.
160	
161	Stored provenance comes from the **value and its representation being written**, not automatically from the provenance of the means of access used to perform the write. Rules for propagation of provenance during byte copies and reinterpretations are not yet fixed.
162	
163	The initial state of a **newly created raw allocation** is wholly uninitialized. Initializing static values or constructing initialized objects are additional operations; it does not follow that all observable static storage starts uninitialized.
164	
165	“All required bytes are initialized” and “these bytes represent a valid value of type T” are two different properties. Constraints on invalid representations, padding bytes, and type alignment will be specified by the corresponding specifications.
166	
167	## 11. Abstract Physical Places
168	
169	A place designates a portion of an allocation's storage. In the minimal kernel, it is defined by that allocation's identity, an offset, and a length. Typed interpretations, subplaces, and fine-grained permissions may extend this representation.
170	
171	Resolution of a means of access to a place must be explicitly defined. It is **partial**: a means of access produces a place only if provenance identifies a **registered allocation (live or dead)** and the address range is spatially contained within it. Producing a resolved place does not, by itself, prove the right to read or write: liveness, initialization, authority, type, alignment, and concurrency are established separately by the applicable rules.
172	
173	## 12. Accesses, Addresses, and Provenance
174	
175	A means of access conceptually contains:
176	
177	- an **address**;
178	- **provenance** identifying the designated allocation;
179	- an **extent** or access length;
180	- an **access authority**;
181	- any other information necessary for its validity.
182	
183	In the elementary memory machine, provenance identifies the allocation; the access discipline in Part IV and following may associate additional constraints with it. **Access authority** (read, write, etc.) is distinct from **deallocation authority**.
184	
185	Resolution uses provenance, **never simply selecting an allocation at the requested numerical address**. A reused address does not validate an old means of access.
186	
187	In the abstract memory machine of Parts II and III, elementary read/write authority is ordered `read ≤ write`; this elementary authority does not replace the discipline of `Observe` and `Modify` modes defined below. In this simplified model, the elementary read-authority condition excludes no access carrying either of those two authorities; substantive rules for observation, modification, and revocation belong to the access discipline. An authority may later become state-dependent and be invalidated.
188	
189	# III. Memory Machine: Accesses and Byte Transitions
190	
191	The following relations describe effects on allocations and bytes, independently of the higher-level permissions subsequently established by the authority discipline.
192	
193	## 13. Allocation Identity and Address Reuse
194	
195	Each creation of an abstract allocation assigns an identity **never reused** during the abstract execution. A dead allocation may remain registered for reasoning purposes without becoming live again.
196	
197	The same numerical address may be reused after the previous storage has been freed. Such reuse never restores the rights or validity of an access carrying the old allocation's provenance.
198	
199	Creating a new allocation does not change pre-existing allocations; read/write/deallocation operations do not create fresh identities unless an explicit later rule provides otherwise.
200	
201	## 14. Restrictive Derivation of Means of Access
202	
203	A **restrictive derivation** of a means of access:
204	
205	- preserves the source allocation's provenance;
206	- designates a **subrange** of the source access;
207	- confers no authority greater than that permitted by the source.
208	
209	In the elementary memory machine, provenance has **allocation granularity**, not field or subrange granularity. Finer-grained rights restrictions are determined by the authority discipline defined in Part IV and following.
210	
211	A valid restrictive derivation is not necessarily the only way to form an address or create a means of access. A safe abstraction may, through mechanisms and invariants yet to be defined, provide new rights to disjoint places; **the creation of rights is not reducible to restrictive derivation**.
212	
213	Forming an address or a means of access is distinct from **using** it. Merely forming an out-of-bounds address is not automatically classified as UB; precise formation and conversion restrictions remain open in Section 19.
214	
215	## 15. Typed Reads and Validity Conditions
216	
217	For an allocation with base `b` and size `s`, an access with address `a` and length `n` is **spatially contained** when `b ≤ a` and `a + n ≤ b + s`. The corresponding ranges are `[a, a+n)` and `[b, b+s)`.
218	
219	A typed read requires all applicable conditions:
220	
221	1. provenance resolves to a **live** allocation;
222	2. the access is **spatially contained** in that allocation;
223	3. the bytes **required** for the representation being read are initialized;
224	4. that representation is valid for the read type;
225	5. read authority is valid;
226	6. the alignment constraints of the read type are satisfied;
227	7. concurrency rules are satisfied.
228	
229	For a zero-length range, the spatial condition permits any address in `[b, b+s]` and requires no initialized bytes. **This does not automatically permit every zero-length typed read**: the operation remains subject to all its other conditions.
230	
231	Violation of a safety obligation of an **unsafe raw** read constitutes UB. A safe read interface must establish the condition or report a defined failure before the dangerous operation.
232	
233	Conditions 4, 6, and 7 are not concretely defined by this kernel; they remain explicit, parameterizable obligations. The choice of how to establish them (static proof, genuinely executable dynamic check, abstraction contract) remains open, subject to Section 4. Thus, kernel theorems alone do not prove the complete validity of an ERN typed read.
234	
235	## 16. Typed Writes and Preservation of the Memory Frame
236	
237	A typed write requires all applicable conditions:
238	
239	1. provenance resolves to a **live** allocation;
240	2. the place is **spatially contained** as specified in Section 15;
241	3. write authority is valid;
242	4. the value and its representation are admissible for the type being written;
243	5. alignment constraints are satisfied;
244	6. concurrency rules are satisfied.
245	
246	A valid write replaces the bytes of the written range **byte by byte** with the supplied representation and its provenance information, then marks the affected bytes initialized. It may initialize a previously uninitialized range. Provenance of the written bytes follows from the representation of the value written, not merely from the provenance of the means of access.
247	
248	Bytes in other allocations and bytes outside the written range in the target allocation remain unchanged; allocation identity and the allocation counter are unaffected. The consequences of replacement for a pre-existing typed value remain to be determined.
249	
250	Conditions 4, 5, and 6 are not concretely defined by this kernel; they remain explicit, parameterizable obligations. A raw write violating a safety obligation is UB; a safe interface must prevent it or produce a defined failure.
251	
252	**Read-after-write and non-interference:** A valid write initializes the bytes of the written range. In the absence of an intervening write or invalidation, **every valid raw byte read of a subrange contained in the written range**, including the entire range, returns exactly the corresponding subsequence of the written contents, including abstract provenance information, subject to the other read conditions. A valid write changes neither the result of a valid read of another allocation nor that of a range disjoint from the written range. These properties concern abstract bytes and do not prejudge the reconstruction of a typed value.
253	
254	## 17. Deallocation and Invalidation of Old Accesses
255	
256	Successful raw deallocation requires:
257	
258	1. an abstract allocation that is **live** and deallocatable;
259	2. **deallocation authority compatible** with that required by the allocation.
260	
261	Compatibility is a semantic relation; it does not necessarily require the two allocator handles to have numerically identical identities, and it is distinct from access provenance.
262	
263	Successful deallocation ends the allocation's validity. Accesses carrying its provenance can no longer read or write that old storage. An attempted double deallocation through the raw operation violates a safety obligation and constitutes UB. A safe abstraction that detects an incompatible attempt before performing a dangerous operation may produce a defined failure; this does not require a universal checked-deallocation primitive.
264	
265	In the elementary memory machine, compatibility is defined between the presented authority and the recorded deallocation token. A library allocator may additionally impose constraints depending on its own state; these do not change the minimal signature of the kernel's compatibility relation.
266	
267	**Validity of derived rights:** The logical invalidation of an object inside an allocation that is still live—for example, a block following an arena reset—is governed by the authorities, anchors, and end-of-use rules in Parts IV through XIV. It does not change the two elementary deallocation conditions in Section 17.
268	
269	## 18. Boundary with Concurrency and Data Races
270	
271	**A *data race* is UB; no execution of safe code can cause one.** This section establishes that guarantee and its interface with the concurrency model, without purporting to define concurrent events and orderings by itself.
272	
273	A *data race* involves conflicting accesses to overlapping memory ranges from concurrent execution contexts, at least one of which is a write and at least one of which is non-atomic, when the ordering relations required by the concurrency model do not order them sufficiently. This criterion becomes fully operational only with the event and synchronization semantics of Spec 2.
274	
275	**Normative boundary:** Spec 2 determines, in particular, the exact definitions of events, conflicts, *happens-before*, atomic operations, and memory orders. The elementary memory machine does not claim that a local access check is sufficient to prove the absence of data races.
276	
277	## 19. Address Conversions and Provenance: Open Boundary
278	
279	ERN must distinguish:
280	
281	1. address calculation that preserves valid provenance;
282	2. extraction of a numerical address representation;
283	3. reconstruction of a means of access from an integer;
284	4. external address spaces and accesses, particularly MMIO;
285	5. representation transformations, particularly tagged pointers and C interoperability.
286	
287	None of these conversions may allow safe code to fabricate dangerous access authority.
288	
289	**Undecided:** exposed provenance, strict provenance, or another model; exact rules for integer–pointer conversions, tagged pointers, and propagation through representation copies. These conversions require a separate definition before any guarantee about reconstructing an access from an integer representation; they are not settled by the simplified provenance of Section 12 alone.
290	
291	---
292	
293	## 20. Relational Semantics and Outcomes
294	
295	**State-domain conditions**, **operation-specific obligations**, **the effect of a valid operation**, and **semantic outcome** must be distinguished.
296	
297	### 20.1 — Normative Transition Relations
298	
299	Raw memory-model operations are interpreted by **transition relations**. Their role is to determine the semantic outcome without assuming that all their obligations can be computed at runtime. Operation names are semantic designations independent of any particular implementation or formalization.
300	
301	In an **admissible** state:
302	
303	- a raw operation satisfying all applicable obligations has a defined `ok` outcome with the specified effect;
304	- violation of a safety obligation of that operation produces a `ub` outcome (Section 6), **including when the obligation is static**;
305	- a `ub` transition does not supply a new ordinary state reusable as a valid step.
306	
307	Memory-machine relations may be deterministic and mathematically total even when certain obligations are not constructively decidable. A classical proof of totality is not a runtime requirement. Modeling a defined failure of resource reservation belongs to the allocator contract: it does not change the classification of violations of safety obligations of raw operations.
308	
309	### 20.2 — Read Values and Effects of Other Operations
310	
311	A valid **byte read** does not modify memory state; its `ok` outcome supplies the sequence of abstract bytes actually read, including provenance. A raw typed read must additionally satisfy type, alignment, and concurrency obligations and subsequent value-reconstruction rules. Unlike operations that only transition the state, a read supplies a value together with its successful outcome.
312	
313	A valid **write** updates its range according to Section 16. A valid **deallocation** ends allocation liveness according to Section 17. A valid **allocation** creates a fresh identity and its storage according to Sections 9, 10, and 13. Non-interference, invalidation, and invariant-preservation properties apply to their `ok` transitions.
314	
315	### 20.3 — Parametric Obligations and Executions
316	
317	Read and write obligations not yet concretely defined are **explicit predicates** of the semantic context: they are not tacitly replaced by `True`.
318	
319	The formalization may distinguish a component with an executable decision procedure from a component whose satisfaction is established by static reasoning or by contract. **This decomposition remains parametric and does not universally prescribe a strategy for each requirement.** It does not permit concurrent safety to be reduced to a simple local test.
320	
321	A normative relation requires **no decision instance** for these predicates to be stated. A computable function may require a decision instance for conditions it evaluates. Obligations and the deallocation-compatibility relation are fixed as **parameters of an execution's context**; obligation predicates may nevertheless depend on the state and operation. The minimal compatibility relation of Section 17 concerns the presented authority and the deallocation token; additional state-dependent contracts belong to the relevant abstraction.
322	
323	# IV. Access Discipline and Aliasing Rules
324	
325	The authority discipline determines which memory operations may be exercised in safe code. A resource may have several identification paths, but only compatible rights may be exercised simultaneously.
326	
327	## 21. Observation and Compiler-Exploitable Stability
328	
329	An observation access (`Observe`) permits ordinary reads of the leaves in its footprint, subject to effectively exercisable rights and read conditions. Multiple compatible observations of the same resource may coexist.
330

1	# ERN — Language Charter v0
2	
3	**Status: Frozen — October 27, 2026**
4	
5	## 1. Identity and Vision
6	
7	ERN `[e.ʁɛn]` is a general-purpose, low-level, systems-oriented programming language designed to combine high performance, extremely fast compilation, modern ergonomics, and precise control over resources.
8	
9	ERN targets systems software, game engines, simulations, development tools, native applications, servers, software infrastructure, and compute-intensive workloads.
10	
11	## 2. Fundamental Objectives
12	
13	ERN pursues five major objectives:
14	
15	1. **Runtime Performance** — produce highly performant native code with controllable costs.
16	2. **Compilation Speed** — minimize development latency and support scalability.
17	3. **Ergonomics** — provide a coherent, readable, expressive, and practical language for systems programming.
18	4. **Safety and Predictability** — enable precise reasoning about operations, resources, and program behavior.
19	5. **Overall Simplicity** — limit unnecessary mechanisms, exceptions, and complexity imposed on users and implementations.
20	
21	No single objective, by itself, justifies a mechanism whose overall cost would be disproportionate.
22	
23	## 3. Cross-Cutting Principles
24	
25	### 3.1 Semantics Before Syntax
26	
27	Language mechanisms are defined semantically before their concrete syntax is finalized.
28	
29	Provisional syntax is permitted for examples and experimentation.
30	
31	### 3.2 Controlled Abstractions
32	
33	Abstractions must make it possible to reason about their runtime costs and provide the necessary optimization opportunities.
34	
35	### 3.3 Explicit Control
36	
37	Significant effects and costs must be understandable and controllable.
38	
39	This does not imply that every operation must necessarily be explicit in the syntax.
40	
41	### 3.4 Language and Library
42	
43	A feature should primarily be implemented in a library when it can be expressed there correctly and efficiently.
44	
45	Its inclusion in the language must be justified by semantic guarantees, compiler requirements, or measurable benefits.
46	
47	### 3.5 Mechanism Coherence
48	
49	Language features must form a coherent system without unjustified proliferation of exceptions or competing mechanisms.
50	
51	### 3.6 Validation Through Concrete Cases
52	
53	Architectural proposals must be tested against representative examples, edge cases, and counterexamples.
54	
55	A feature must not be adopted solely because it is novel or exists in another language.
56	
57	## 4. Memory Model and Safety
58	
59	ERN aims to provide a memory model that enables precise low-level control, efficient resource management, and clearly defined safety guarantees.
60	
61	### 4.1 Safety Contract
62	
63	Safe ERN code must guarantee:
64	
65	1. **Spatial memory safety**.
66	2. **Temporal memory safety**.
67	3. **Absence of reads of uninitialized values**.
68	4. **Absence of type confusion**.
69	5. **Absence of data races**.
70	
71	These guarantees also depend on the contracts of any unsafe abstractions being respected.
72	
73	The safety contract does not automatically guarantee the absence of:
74	
75	- Memory or resource leaks.
76	- Deadlocks.
77	- Stack overflows.
78	
79	These exclusions do not prevent the language or its libraries from providing mechanisms for prevention, detection, or diagnosis.
80	
81	### 4.2 Memory Model
82	
83	Rules governing values, storage locations, references, memory accesses, resources, invalidation, and unsafe operations will be established by the memory model specification.
84	
85	The safety contract must distinguish guarantees applicable to safe code from the obligations associated with unsafe operations.
86	
87	The charter does not presuppose any particular model of ownership, borrowing, regions, or destruction.
88	
89	## 5. Concurrency and Asynchrony
90	
91	ERN aims to support efficient concurrent and parallel programming compatible with its memory safety guarantees.
92	
93	The design must accommodate different execution and scheduling models without unnecessarily imposing a single runtime.
94	
95	Guarantees concerning sharing, synchronization, atomicity, suspension, and cancellation will be defined in the relevant specifications.
96	
97	## 6. Control Flow and Errors
98	
99	ERN must provide coherent semantics for expressions, functions, branches, loops, scopes, and control transfers.
100	
101	Error handling, propagation, abnormal termination, and cleanup mechanisms must be compatible with the memory model.
102	
103	Their precise forms and rules belong to the specifications.
104	
105	## 7. Types and Data Representation
106	
107	ERN aims to provide an expressive type system suitable for systems programming.
108	
109	The language must enable appropriate control over memory representations and efficient data-oriented programming.
110	
111	The specific mechanisms for typing, layouts, views, and data abstractions will be determined by the corresponding specifications.
112	
113	## 8. Arithmetic and Vector Computation
114	
115	ERN aims to provide performant numerical and vector computation capabilities.
116	
117	The semantics of arithmetic operations, conversions, floating-point operations, and SIMD must be sufficiently precise to enable optimizations while preserving the language's guarantees.
118	
119	## 9. Generics and Metaprogramming
120	
121	ERN must support the construction of reusable abstractions and the execution of computations at compile time.
122	
123	Generics, compile-time evaluation (`comptime`), reflection, and generation must be designed consistently with the type system, memory model, and fast-compilation objectives.
124	
125	## 10. Modules and Interoperability
126	
127	ERN must support modularity and efficient interoperability with native environments.
128	
129	Interoperability with C is a priority objective.
130	
131	Guarantees concerning external interfaces, calling conventions, binary representation, and linking will be established in the appropriate specifications.
132	
133	## 11. Compiler and Tooling
134	
135	ERN aims to eventually provide a self-hosted compiler.
136	
137	Its objectives include a performant compilation architecture, precise diagnostics, modern tooling, and the ability to leverage different optimization and code generation strategies.
138	
139	Decisions concerning intermediate representations, backends, bootstrapping, incremental compilation, and hot reload will be based on technical evaluation and experimentation.
140	
141	The internal compiler architecture must not implicitly alter the normative semantics of the language.
142	
143	## 12. Validation Criteria
144	
145	Major decisions must be evaluated according to their impact on:
146	
147	- Runtime performance.
148	- Compilation speed.
149	- Ergonomics.
150	- Safety and predictability guarantees.
151	- Overall complexity of the language and its implementation.
152	
153	Evaluations may rely on stress-test cases, prototypes, benchmarks, and formal models.
154	
155	Adopted decisions must comply with the principles of this charter.
156	
157	## 13. Specifications and Formalization
158	
159	### 13.1 Document Responsibilities
160	
161	The charter establishes the objectives, principles, and design order.
162	
163	Specifications establish language mechanisms, their behaviors, and their normative guarantees.
164	
165	A specification may cover multiple closely related mechanisms.
166	
167	No subdivision into additional documents is required unless necessary.
168	
169	### 13.2 Specification Content
170	
171	Each specification defines, as appropriate to its scope:
172	
173	- The concepts involved.
174	- Semantic rules.
175	- Permitted and forbidden behaviors.
176	- Invariants.
177	- Examples and counterexamples.
178	- Stress-test cases and their expected verdicts.
179	- Interactions with other specifications.
180	
181	### 13.3 Formalization
182	
183	Lean 4 is used progressively as a tool for designing, evaluating, and verifying the semantic properties of the language.
184	
185	Formal models accompany the design of mechanisms and enable examination of their guarantees before stabilization.
186	
187	Validated specifications constitute the normative reference; formal models must remain consistent with their rules.
188	
189	### 13.4 Syntax
190	
191	Abstract syntax and provisional notations may precede the final grammar.
192	
193	The normative grammar is established after the corresponding semantic mechanisms have been stabilized.
194	
195	### 13.5 Sources of Truth
196	
197	Design documents may contain hypotheses, alternatives, and historical analyses.
198	
199	These documents are not authoritative for implementation.
200	
201	The validated charter and validated normative specifications constitute the official references for the language.
202	
203	Approved technical implementation documents must comply with these references.
204	
205	## 14. Evolution and Stability
206	
207	Charter v0 is frozen upon validation and takes precedence over specifications in the normative hierarchy.
208	
209	Any modification to its principles or commitments requires an explicit, justified revision of the charter.
210	
211	Specifications may evolve according to their modification procedures without contradicting the charter.
212	
213	Language compatibility and versioning policies will be refined during its development.
214	
215	## 15. Long-Term Vision
216	
217	ERN aims to provide a durable foundation for an ecosystem of libraries, runtimes, tools, and native applications.
218	
219	Its architecture must accommodate the evolution of language capabilities and hardware platforms without sacrificing its coherence, efficiency, or fundamental principles.
220
